   As shown above, it has been illustrated that low thermal conductivity, low emissivity, and low mass
density are the most important parameters for an insulation system utilized in a long-term aerospace
application. These are the key properties that need to be measured for any insulation system. In addition,
low thermal diffusivity, low CTE, and an ability to accommodate the thermal distortions induced by large
thermal gradients are important considerations.
   The current state of the art suggests that the use of a high vacuum with highly polished wall surfaces
with or without an MLI system could provide the required insulation needs for lightweight long-term
cryogenic applications. The MLI provides additional insulation against radiation heat transfer relative to a
simple vacuum jacket. However, either system is very sensitive and dependent on maintaining a very high
level of vacuum. Any degradation in the vacuum level significantly degrades the insulating properties,
leading to mission failure. Any currently available foam-based system, possibly including current
aerogels, may require continued enhancement in their thermomechanical properties for aircraft
application. Foam-based insulation may be appropriate for short-duration applications and possibly as a
supplementary system for longer duration applications.

                     4.2 Potential Structural Tank Materials and Architectures

   The storage of LH2 in a lightweight tank provides significant challenges in itself. The lower density of
the hydrogen fuel results in the need for a higher volume storage vessel relative to other fuels. Mechanical
tank loads are derived from (1) the difference between the pressure within the tank and the ambient
conditions, (2) fuel weight, (3) vehicle acceleration loads, (4) fuel slosh due to aircraft maneuvers, and (5)
tank system weight and its supports. Fuel slosh is bound to be encountered as the aircraft maneuvers or as
it encounters air turbulence during the flight.
   The internal tank pressure will have to be maintained at a constant absolute pressure in order to
maintain the hydrogen in a liquid state. The pressure will aid in pumping hydrogen from the tank to the
power source also. Hall and Silverstein (1955) have suggested that 2 atm (200 kPa, 29 psia) would be
adequate for pumping fuel at a cruise condition for an aircraft. It has also been documented by Petty
(2002) that the space shuttle ET operates in the pressure range of 220 to 230 kPa (32 to 34 psia), which is
close to the suggested range by Hall and Silverstein. Furthermore, the designed tank weight increases
with increasing operating pressure. Thus, it is highly desirable to keep the tank pressure as low as
possible, as noted by Reynolds (1955). Typically, GH2 is used as the pressurant for LH2.
   Two important criteria for the tank wall include material selection and wall architecture. Many
options are available, and these are discussed in the following sections. Advantages and disadvantages of
various options are discussed, and guidelines are provided for choosing an optimum system.



NASA/TM—2006-214346                        18    4.2.1 Tank wall material selection.—Clearly it is desirable to use materials that possess high
strength, high fracture toughness, and high stiffness, as well as low density and low permeation to liquid
and gaseous hydrogen; however, no single material provides all these attributes simultaneously.
Consequently, material performance indices associated with these properties, such as those given in
table II, must be used to identify the best material candidates for tank wall construction. Among these
parameters, strength and density tend to dominate the design criteria. Figure 7 shows strength versus mass
density for various engineering materials. In this case, materials in the upper left corner are preferable.
Composite materials exhibit high specific strength relative to metals and are quite suitable for aerospace
applications. In particular, it is apparent from figure 7 that continuous-fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP)
composites provide the highest strength yet lightest choice. However, the use of continuous-fiber-
reinforced composite materials most likely will involve higher initial manufacturing costs. As per
figure 7, the materials that have the sufficient strength and acceptable low density are PMCs and metallic
materials. Ceramic materials also offer high specific strength, but because of their low fracture toughness,
they are not viable for a tank wall material.
  A potential lower cost alternative to continuous-fiber-reinforced composites may be discontinuous
reinforced metallic composites (DRX), specifically discontinuous reinforced aluminum (DRA) as
described by Miracle (2001). DRAs are essentially isotropic and can be manufactured using less
expensive techniques such as casting. Figure 8 illustrates the specific modulus relative to specific
strength. In this figure, materials closer to upper right corner are desirable. DRX materials compare well
with polymer-based composite systems. The DRX materials have the added benefit of extremely low (if
not negligible) hydrogen gas permeability issues typically associated with polymer matrix composite
systems.

## 1. worden2011externaltankprogramlegacy pages 1-3 (Context ID: pqac-00000072)

AIAA Technical Paper – External Tank Program – Legacy of
                         Success


                  Jeffery C. Pilet0F1, Dawn Diecidue-Conners1F2, Michelle Worden2F3, Michelle Guillot3F4
                    Lockheed Martin Space Systems Company, New Orleans, LA, 70129
                                               and

                                         Kenneth Welzyn4F5
                     NASA, Marshall Space Flight Center, Huntsville, AL 35812



   The largest single element of Space Shuttle is the External Tank (ET), which serves as the structural
   backbone of the vehicle during ascent and provides liquid propellants to the Orbiter’s three Main
   Engines.  The ET absorbs most of the seven million pounds of thrust exerted by the Solid Rocket
   Boosters and Main Engines. The design evolved through several block changes, reducing weight each
   time. Because the tank flies to orbital velocity with the Space Shuttle Orbiter, minimization of weight
    is mandatory, to maximize payload performance. The initial configuration, the standard weight tank,
   weighed 76,000 pounds and was an aluminum 2219 structure. The light weight tank weighed 66,000
   pounds and flew 86 missions. The super light weight tank weighed 58,500 pounds and was primarily
   an aluminum-lithium structure.  The  final configuration and low weight enabled system  level
   performance sufficient for assembly of the International Space Station in a high inclination orbit, vital
   for international cooperation. Another significant challenge was the minimization of ice formation on
   the cryogenic tanks.  This was essential due to the system configuration and the choice of ceramic
   thermal protection system materials on the Orbiter.  Ice would have been a major debris hazard.
   Spray on foam  insulation  materials  served  multiple  functions  including  thermal  insulation,
   conditioning of cryogenic propellants, and thermal protection for the tank structure during ascent and
   entry.   The  tank  is  large, and unique  manufacturing  facilities,  tooling, and  handling, and
   transportation operations were developed. Weld processes and tooling evolved with the design as it
   matured through several block changes. Non Destructive Evaluation methods were used to assure
    integrity of welds and thermal protection system materials.  The aluminum-lithium alloy was used
   near the end of the program and weld processes and weld repair techniques had to be refined.
   Development and implementation of friction stir welding was a substantial technology development
   incorporated during the Program. Automated thermal protection system application processes were
   developed for the majority of the tank surface.  Material obsolescence was an issue throughout the
   multi-decade program.  Process controls were implemented to assure cleanliness in the production
   environment, to control contaminants, and to preclude corrosion. Each tank was accepted via rigorous
   inspections, including non-destructive evaluation techniques, proof testing, and all systems testing. In
   the post STS-107 era, the project focused on ascent debris risk reduction. This was accomplished via
   stringent process controls, post flight assessment using substantially improved imagery, and selective
   redesigns.  These efforts were supported with a number of test programs to simulate combined
   environments. The debris risk was reduced by two orders of magnitude. During this time a major
   natural  disaster was overcome when  hurricane Katrina damaged  the manufacturing  facility.
   Numerous lessons from these efforts, the manufacturing and material processing issues, the key design
    features, and evolution of the design will be discussed.

   HE Space Shuttle’s External Tank (ET) is a highly evolved and optimizedT system that serves as the structural backbone of the Space Transportation
System (STS) launch vehicle (Figure 1). Several major design changes to the
ET have occurred since the  first flight of the Shuttle 30 years ago, with
emphasis  on  improving  overall  system  payload  performance,  reducing
manufacturing flow time, and improving design robustness.  Through the
process of evolving the ET design, many challenges were experienced and
ultimately overcome by a very proud, resilient, and cohesive team consisting
of National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA) and Lockheed
Martin engineers from NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) in
Huntsville AL and the Michoud Assembly Facility (MAF) in New Orleans,
LA. The purpose of this paper is to provide an overview of some of the more
challenging issues and resulting lessons learned to potentially benefit the
follow-on Space Launch System (SLS) core stage booster program. The paper
provides an overview of the ET design, a discussion of the major structural
design evolutions, innovative welding techniques, the debris minimization
efforts that occurred after the Columbia accident, and several key technical
challenges that were recently experienced and overcome.                                                                           Figure 1: STS on Pad
                                               II.  Design Overview

   The ET contains and delivers propellants for the Orbiter's three main engines during the launch phase and serves
as the structural backbone for the Orbiter and two Solid Rocket Boosters (SRBs) to make up the Space Shuttle flight
vehicle. The liquid oxygen (LO2) tank volume is 19,463 cubic feet and contains approximately 1,385,000 pounds of
oxidizer. The liquid hydrogen (LH2) tank volume is 52,371 cubic feet and contains approximately 231,000 pounds
of propellant fuel. These volumes include a 3% ullage provision.

   The ET structure must accommodate complex load paths in that the SRB thrust loads will be induced forward at
the Intertank while the Orbiter thrust loads will be induced at aft ET/Orbiter attachment points. The SRB thrust will
be as high as 2.9 million pounds each at sea level and the Orbiter's three main engines will develop as much as
375,000 pounds thrust each at sea level.

   Three primary structures make up the ET; a LO2 tank, an Intertank, and a LH2 tank (Figure 2). Since the ET is
the only expendable element of the Space Shuttle, the design philosophy has been to minimize active or moving

                                   2. Historical Background

                           The main contributing factor to the discovery of hydrogen as an element in the late
                           18th century was its flammability. It was immediately identified as a potential fuel and it
                      was first used as such early in the 19th century [3].
                           The liquefaction of hydrogen was achieved late in the 19th century [4], yet due to
                          handling issues related to the cryogenic temperatures, liquid hydrogen was not used as
                          a fuel until 1955, when a United States Air Force (USAF) B-57B Canberra bomber was
                          modified to carry a stainless steel LH2 tank on its wingtip that was feeding one of the two
                             engines. The experiment was successful, with the aircraft flying for about 20 min with one
                           engine running on LH2 [5].
                            The 1960s saw the first large scale use of LH2 as a rocket fuel. The first successful use of
                    LH2 as a rocket propellant was the Atlas-Centaur, with the Centaur cryogenic upper stage
                        used on top of the Atlas booster, with the first successful flight on 27 November 1963 [6],
                      shown in Figure 1a. Cryogenic upper stages were also considered for the Saturn family
                             of rockets of the Apollo program, initially with the S-IV stage of the Saturn I using the
                       same RL-10 engines as the Centaur [6]. The RL-10 engines of the S-IV were later replaced
                       by the J-2 engines resulting in the S-IVB upper stage, used as the second on the Saturn
                           IB and as the third stage of the Saturn V rocket. The Saturn V, shown in Figure 1b, had aAerospace 2024, 11, 161                                                                                                          3 of 31



                           cryogenic second stage as well, the S-II, and it was powered by five J-2 engines [7]. The
                         development of the Space Transportation System (STS), better known as the space shuttle,
                             started before the end of the Apollo program, with the maiden flight on 12 April 1981,
                      shown in Figure 1c. The STS comprises three main components: the space shuttle orbiter
                        where the crew is located, the two reusable solid rocket boosters (SRB) that provide the extra
                              thrust needed for take-off, and the external tank (ET) where the liquid hydrogen and liquid
                         oxygen propellants for the main engines are stored [8]. The space shuttle program has laid
                             the foundation for the development of the currently used launch vehicle for manned space
                             exploration, the Space Launch System (SLS) of the Artemis program, shown in Figure 1d.
                     Many space shuttle components were redesigned and repurposed for the SLS including the
                              solid rocket boosters, with a more powerful version using five segments of fuel instead of
                               four, the RS-25 main engines, and the external tank, which was modified to serve as the
                             core stage. The main redesign of the ET was the replacement of the liquid oxygen tank with
                           a cylindrical one, with the liquid hydrogen tank remaining mostly unchanged. The second
                             stage is the same as the Delta IV rocket, again using liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen as
                              propellants, and it is powered by a single RL-10 engine, the same as the Centaur [9].

                                       4Notch-sensitive properties, such as tensile ductility, fracture toughness, or fatigue crack growth,
of rolled Al alloys are governed by the grain size/morphology and the size/spacing of intergranular
precipitates [refs. 19 to 21]. The fracture behavior is dominated by the nucleation and growth of
voids at coarse constituent particles, particularly when GBs are continuously decorated with the
second phase [refs. 22 and 23]. Mechanistically, microvoid formation and coalescence at such
intergranular particles is responsible for fracture initiation and propagation under both monotonic
and cyclic loading. For example, stringers of coarse Al2Cu particles, preferentially aligned along
elongated GBs, caused premature fracture in flow-formed 2219 cylinders [ref. 24]. Reduced tensile
ductility was attributed to the formation of microcracks around individual particles that rapidly
coalesced into much larger intergranular cracks.
In the elongated grain structures typical of 2219 thick plate, there is a high proportion of GB area
oriented in the rolling (L-LT) plane. Decoration of these GBs with copious Al2Cu θ-phase will
exert a strong influence on mechanical properties evaluated in the ST orientation. In this case,
cyclic loading in the ST direction tends to result in failure by a combination of trans- and inter-
granular fracture. As illustrated in Figure 2, the crack path typically lies in the rolling (L-LT) plane,
traverses grains, and deviates towards clusters of Cu-rich particles located on favorably oriented
GBs [data courtesy of Dawicke]. Trans-granular fracture involves ductile rupture through the
matrix, whereas inter-granular fracture includes brittle cleavage through θ-phase particles.

         Marshall   Space  Flight  Center  has developed   a new TS aging  treatment    that  consists   of exposures
at 132 °C (270  °F)/20  hr + 138 °C (280  °F)/42   hr. TS  aging  can  achieve   the  same YS  levels  as those

failed  to  pass  simulated    service   testing)  were  found  acceptable    for use  in the SLWT  program.

        These  material   properties   were  improved   by constraining   T 1 nucleation   and growth   at subgrain
boundaries,   which  permitted   more  uniform   distribution    of T 1 throughout    the  alloy.

 13. ABSTRACT   (Maximum  200 words)
 Marshall  Space  Flight  Center  has developed   a two-step  (TS)  artificial  aging  technique   that  can
 significantly   enhance   cryogenic   fracture   toughness   and  resistance   to  stress  corrosion   cracking
 (SCC)  in aluminum-copper-lithium     alloy 2195. The new TS aging  treatment   consists  of exposures
  at 132  °C (270  °F)/20   hr + 138 °C (280  °F)/42   hr,  which  can  be  readily   applied   to  flight  hardware
 production.   TS  aging  achieves   the  same  yield  strength   levels   as  conventional    aging,  while
 provMing much improved   ductility  in the short transverse  direction.  After TS aging,  five previously
  rejected    lots  of  alloy  2195   (lots  950M029B,    960M030F,    960M030J,   960M030K,    and  960M030L)
 passed  simulated   service  testing  for use  in the  super lightweight   tank program.  Each  lot exhibited
 higher   fracture   toughness    at  cryogenic   temperature   than   at  ambient   temperature.    Their  SCC
 resistance  was  also  enhanced.   All SCC  specimens   passed  the minimum   10-day  requirement    in
 3.5-percent  sodium  chloride  alternate  immersion   at a stress  of 45  ksi. The SCC  lives ranged  from
 57 to 83 days,  with an average  of 70 days.

From text 'witzell1977evaluationofmechanical pages 24-28'.

WE Witzell. Evaluation of mechanical property data on the 2219 aluminum alloy and application of the data to the design of liquid hydrogen tankage. Unknown journal, 1977.

The excerpt reports plane-stress critical crack-intensity data, designated Kc rather than KIC, for 2219 aluminum alloy and TIG weldments. The table gives longitudinal base-metal Kc values of 50 at room temperature and 69 at 20 K, with transverse values of 47 and 68, respectively. Weld Kc values are lower: 33 at room temperature and 45 at 20 K; chemically milled weld values are 33 and 47. The unit label is OCR-corrupted in the excerpt but is intended to be MPa√m. The text explicitly identifies these as static plane-stress critical crack-intensity factors obtained with center-notched specimens, and states that weldments have lower plane-stress fracture toughness than the base metal. The tensile-property table indicates room-temperature base-metal yield and ultimate strengths of 385 and 460 MPa, versus 506 and 684 MPa at 20 K. Corresponding weld values are 135 and 262 MPa at room temperature, and 249 and 458 MPa at 20 K; the prose confirms that cryogenic strength increases while weld strength remains below base-metal strength. This excerpt contains no 77 K test results or evidence that 77 K data were directly measured; it does mention liquid-hydrogen-temperature crack-growth testing, but not imported surface-crack plots.

From text 'witzell1977evaluationofmechanical pages 67-71'.

WE Witzell. Evaluation of mechanical property data on the 2219 aluminum alloy and application of the data to the design of liquid hydrogen tankage. Unknown journal, 1977.

The excerpt provides Table 10, a fracture-analysis material-property summary for 2219-T87 aluminum. It reports plane-orientation and temperature-specific data for LT and TL parent material at 0.127 cm thickness, plus welded material at 0.318 cm thickness. The listed conditions are 20 K and room temperature (R.T.). The table labels fracture parameters as Kf rather than Kc or KIC, with units rendered by OCR as MPa sqrt(m). For through cracks, the parent-metal values are 241 MPa sqrt(m) at 20 K and 64.8 MPa sqrt(m) at room temperature in LT, and 201 and 65.9 MPa sqrt(m) in TL. Surface-crack Kf values are 192 and 50.6 MPa sqrt(m) in LT, and 160 and 44.0 MPa sqrt(m) in TL. Weld Kf entries are blank in the reproduced table. Ultimate and yield stresses are also given: parent ultimate stress is 648 MPa at 20 K and 434 MPa at room temperature, while weld ultimate stress is 365 and 241 MPa. The excerpt contains graphical test results rather than the requested plane-stress Kc table or tensile-property tables. It documents 2219-T87 aluminum in the LT direction, with surface-crack and through-crack results plotted against specimen thickness. The figures include cryogenic test conditions identified as approximately −320°F and −423°F, corresponding to about 77 K and 20 K, respectively. The plots distinguish surface cracks from through cracks and mark cases where the net stress exceeds yield. Thickness is given in both inches and centimeters. These pages therefore support that cryogenic crack-related data were presented graphically, including data near 77 K and 20 K, but they do not provide exact Kc values in MPa√m, a complete 50/69 RT-to-20 K table, or the parent-material and TIG-weld tensile values cited in the question. ## pqac-00000084

From text 'masters1974deepflawsin pages 44-48'.

JN Masters, WL Engstrom, and WD Bixler. Deep flaws in weldments of aluminum and titanium. Unknown journal, 1974.

The excerpt discusses static fracture and leak-before-fail behavior of 2219-T87 aluminum weldments, rather than reproducing the NASA CR-145140/Witzell 1977 tensile-strength or plane-stress Kc table requested. It reports applied-stress versus flaw-size results at room temperature, 78 K, and 20 K for 1.60, 2.67, and 7.62 mm weldments. Thin specimens generally leaked or broke through before fracture; in the 7.62 mm material, fracture before leakage occurred only at stresses near or above yield at room temperature and 78 K. {"answer": "# Cryogenic aluminum-alloy evidence for propellant tanks

**The distinction is between a material test and a tank’s operating temperature.** Liquid nitrogen testing near **77 K** (−196 °C, −320 °F) is common in alloy screening; liquid-hydrogen testing near **20 K** (−253 °C, −423 °F) addresses the colder service condition. A paper specifying a 20 K hydrogen tank does **not**, by itself, establish that its alloy coupons were tested at 20 K. The public record is detailed for some NASA programs but does not support a uniform, vehicle-by-vehicle list of 77 K and 20 K qualification results. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000065)

| Program or study | What the documentation establishes | Specimen-test temperature and measured property; source |
|---|---|---|
| **Space Shuttle external tank and super-lightweight tank (SLWT)** | The original tank used **2219**; **2195 Al–Li** replaced it in substantial portions of the lighter tank. Production acceptance encompassed material allowables, welds, inspection and proof tests, not merely parent-metal strength. Welding difficulties later led some domes and ogives back to 2219. | Chen and colleagues tested 2195 fracture specimens at **ambient and 77 K**, measuring strength and cryogenic fracture toughness; the reported SLWT minimum cryogenic toughness was **30 ksi√in**. Separately, a published lot-acceptance guideline was **fracture-toughness ratio, FTR = cryogenic/ambient toughness >1**. For lot 950M029B, conventional aging gave **25.40/30.04 = 0.85**; two-step aging gave **33.74/30.44 = 1.11**, in ksi√in at 77 K/ambient. The treatment improved the cryogenic value while controlling detrimental subgrain-boundary T₁ precipitates. These are **77 K results, not 20 K toughness results**. NASA/TM-2002-211546; NASA/TM-2002-211547; Chen *et al.*, DOI **10.1361/105994998770347576**; Chen and Stanton, DOI **10.1557/proc-551-285**. (pqac-00000072, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000062, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000067, pqac-00000075) |
| **Shuttle-related 2195 friction-stir-weld development** | Weld qualification is distinct from the foregoing plate-lot toughness criterion. Lockheed Martin tested 2195/2195 and 2219/2195 combinations, including surface-crack-tension specimens. | **Room temperature and −423 °F (≈20 K)** tensile tests were reported. The paper describes a **1.6 cryogenic/room-temperature weld-strength enhancement factor**, weld strength approaching parent-metal strength at 20 K, and improved surface-crack-tension performance relative to fusion welding; **1.6 is a strength ratio, not FTR**. Kinchen, Li and Adams, “Mechanical Properties of Friction Stir Welds in Al2195-T8” (1999). The ET program history reports approximately **80% base-metal-strength** FSW joints versus **40–50%** for fusion welds, without assigning those summary percentages to a particular test temperature. (pqac-00000078, pqac-00000031) |
| **SLS core stage** | SLS uses **2219** for its cryogenic tank structure; development work also investigated possible 2195 dome gores. A NASA safety assessment examined the short-transverse weakness of commercial *thick 2219-T87 plate*, an important caveat to using favorable longitudinal properties as design allowables. | Hales reports **full-thickness short-transverse tensile tests at 20 °C, −196 °C (≈77 K), and −253 °C (≈20 K)**, measuring yield strength, ultimate strength and fracture elongation. Through-thickness variations and intermetallic-particle clustering affected fracture. This is **plate characterization**, not a published 20 K toughness ratio for a completed SLS tank or its FSW seams. **NASA/TM-20230006220**, NESC-RP-21-01721; related Medders *et al.*, **NASA/TM-20230018439**. (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000079, pqac-00000074, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000076) |
| **Delta IV; Atlas V/Centaur; Vulcan** | Reviews discuss FSW in launch-tank manufacture and identify **Al–Li** use in Atlas V’s Centaur. Those statements do not identify a common alloy, test method or qualification campaign for all three vehicles. | **No attributable 77 K/20 K coupon-property table, FTR, or leak-before-break demonstration for these named programs was established in the retrieved papers.** Their use of cryogenic propellants cannot supply a missing specimen-test temperature. (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000057) |
| **Falcon 9** | A published review identifies **Al–Li 2198** sheet/plate in its stages; another describes friction-stir-welded aluminum-alloy tank manufacture. Falcon 9’s stage propellants are **LOX/kerosene rather than liquid hydrogen**: Shuttle LH₂-tank 20 K results must not be assigned to it. | **No Falcon-9-specific 77 K or 20 K tensile, fracture-toughness, weld-strength or leak-before-break dataset was verified** in the retrieved literature. Review: Ablakatov *et al.*, DOI **10.31643/2022/6445.34**. (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000057) |
| **Ariane 5** | A 1996 weldment paper states that **AA2219 was selected for Ariane V**; it studies 2219 weld microstructure, hardness, tensile properties and weld efficiency. | That paper **does not document a 77 K or 20 K Ariane-5 tank-coupon qualification series**. Rao *et al.*, DOI **10.1007/BF02744827**. (pqac-00000043) |
| **Ariane 6** | An MT Aerospace conference paper specifies, for the upper-module tanks, **2195 cylinder/dome segments** and **2219 rings and manhole hardware**; its lower-module components instead specify **2195 domes** and **2219 cylinders and rings**. It describes FSW and development/qualification activities, including panel and structural testing. | **20 K to room temperature for LH₂** and **90 K to room temperature for LOX** are stated **tank design ranges**, *not disclosed coupon-test temperatures*. The paper does not furnish a 77 K/20 K alloy toughness ratio or test matrix. Merino *et al.*, “Ariane 6—Tanks & Structures for the New European Launcher,” **Deutscher Luft- und Raumfahrtkongress 2017, Document ID 450255**. (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000066, pqac-00000039) |
| **H-IIA, H-IIB and H3** | A Mitsubishi Heavy Industries paper describes H-IIB tank/FSW development based on H-IIA hardware. A subscale welded tank was pressure-tested to **more than 1.5 times expected flight stress**; it also reports larger-scale axial and circumferential weld demonstrations. | Its **−253 °C LH₂** and **−183 °C LOX** values identify **propellant service environments**, not recorded tensile or toughness coupon-test temperatures. The accessible paper does not substantiate a particular H-IIA/H3 aluminum grade or a 77 K/20 K FTR. Goto *et al.*, “Highly Reliable Tank Structure of H-IIB Launch Vehicle” (2005). **H3-specific qualification values were not verified.** (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045) |
| **Chinese launch vehicles** | A review traces tank alloys **5A06 → 2A14/2219** and explicitly identifies **2219** for the **CZ-5 LH₂ tank**; it discusses weld defects and residual stress as qualification concerns. | It recommends more systematic properties testing at and below **77 K**, but supplies **no attributable CZ-5 77 K-versus-20 K coupon series**, toughness ratio, or leak-before-break result. Nor does it establish that a particular Chinese launcher adopted **Al–Li** in place of these grades. Qiu *et al.*, DOI **10.3390/met11071101**. (pqac-00000076, pqac-00000030) |
| **NASA thin-wall LH₂ *aircraft* tank investigation** | Unlike a conceptual tank comparison, Convair’s NASA-sponsored study generated **2219-T87 parent-metal and TIG-weld** data for a hypothetical aircraft tank and used flaw-growth calculations to examine service life. | **Room-temperature and actual 20 K LH₂-cryostat tests** measured yield/ultimate tensile strength, *plane-stress* crack resistance **Kc**, fatigue and crack growth. Parent-metal yield/ultimate rose from approximately **385/460 to 506/684 MPa**; weld values rose from **135/262 to 249/458 MPa**. Longitudinal parent-metal **Kc: 50→69 MPa√m**; weld **Kc: 33→45 MPa√m**. These must **not** be relabeled plane-strain *K*IC. The report also reproduces −320 °F and −423 °F surface-/through-crack information; its newly reported tensile and Kc comparisons are specifically room temperature versus **20 K**. Witzell, **NASA/CR-145140** (1977). (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000080, pqac-00000083) |
| **NASA aircraft material screening; Airbus and DLR studies** | NASA’s **2050-T84** comparison tests show why a 77 K material screen is not an LH₂-temperature qualification: compact-tension results vary by crack orientation, and the authors specifically request future **20 K** testing. Aircraft tank design papers and Airbus Cryoplane concepts address structural sizing, thermal insulation and operation, rather than establishing Airbus/DLR alloy-coupon qualification data. | At **75 °F versus −320 °F (≈77 K)**, 2050 conditional toughness **KQJIC** was **38.4→32.4 ksi√in (L–T)**, **24.8→28.2 (T–L)** and **37.7→44.4 (L–S)**: ratios **0.84, 1.14 and 1.18**. **All failed the cited ASTM toughness-validity requirements**; they are comparative, not certified *K*IC values. **NASA/TM-2011-217163**. Gomez and Smith’s aircraft sizing study, DOI **10.1016/j.ast.2019.105438**, specifies a **22.5 K modeled tank condition**, not a specimen test. The retrieved Airbus/DLR-related accounts do **not** provide a verified proprietary 77 K/20 K aluminum-alloy test matrix. (pqac-00000068, pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070, pqac-00000077, pqac-00000073) |

**Leak-before-break requires separate evidence.** NASA’s aircraft-tank review, **NASA/TM-2006-214346**, presents the material-selection indices *K*IC/σf for yield-before-break and **(*K*IC)²/σf** for leak-before-break. An index is **not** evidence that a particular launcher passed a pressurized, flawed-tank test. Earlier 2219 pressure-vessel work instead explicitly studied proof loads, ligament penetration and residual cyclic life across conditions down to **20 K** (**NASA/CR-135036**); weldment flaw tests at about **78 K and 20 K** observed leakage before fracture in many configurations but also identified thickness- and stress-dependent exceptions. These studies support examining flaws, welds, wall thickness and operating load together rather than declaring an alloy intrinsically “leak-before-break.” (pqac-00000063, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000050)

**Bottom line:** The most traceable progression is **77 K plate screening and SLWT 2195 lot acceptance → 20 K testing of selected welds, thick 2219 plate and aircraft-tank materials → component proof, flaw-growth and leak assessment**. It is *not* documented as one identical test sequence across the listed launchers. In particular, a 20 K LH₂ service specification, a 77 K alloy paper, and a room-temperature weld result cannot be combined into a claimed program-specific 20 K qualification without a report that actually connects them. (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000078, pqac-00000079, pqac-00000065, pqac-00000038)"}

| **NASA aircraft material screening; Airbus and DLR studies** | NASA’s **2050-T84** comparison tests show why a 77 K material screen is not an LH₂-temperature qualification: compact-tension results vary by crack orientation, and the authors specifically request future **20 K** testing. Aircraft tank design papers and Airbus Cryoplane concepts address structural sizing, thermal insulation and operation, rather than establishing Airbus/DLR alloy-coupon qualification data. | At **75 °F versus −320 °F (≈77 K)**, 2050 conditional toughness **KQJIC** was **38.4→32.4 ksi√in (L–T)**, **24.8→28.2 (T–L)** and **37.7→44.4 (L–S)**: ratios **0.84, 1.14 and 1.18**. **All failed the cited ASTM toughness-validity requirements**; they are comparative, not certified *K*IC values. **NASA/TM-2011-217163**. Gomez and Smith’s aircraft sizing study, DOI **10.1016/j.ast.2019.105438**, specifies a **22.5 K modeled tank condition**, not a specimen test. The retrieved Airbus/DLR-related accounts do **not** provide a verified proprietary 77 K/20 K aluminum-alloy test matrix. (pqac-00000068, pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070, pqac-00000077, pqac-00000073) |

**Leak-before-break requires separate evidence.** NASA’s aircraft-tank review, **NASA/TM-2006-214346**, presents the material-selection indices *K*IC/σf for yield-before-break and **(*K*IC)²/σf** for leak-before-break. An index is **not** evidence that a particular launcher passed a pressurized, flawed-tank test. Earlier 2219 pressure-vessel work instead explicitly studied proof loads, ligament penetration and residual cyclic life across conditions down to **20 K** (**NASA/CR-135036**); weldment flaw tests at about **78 K and 20 K** observed leakage before fracture in many configurations but also identified thickness- and stress-dependent exceptions. These studies support examining flaws, welds, wall thickness and operating load together rather than declaring an alloy intrinsically “leak-before-break.” (pqac-00000063, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000050)

**Bottom line:** The most traceable progression is **77 K plate screening and SLWT 2195 lot acceptance → 20 K testing of selected welds, thick 2219 plate and aircraft-tank materials → component proof, flaw-growth and leak assessment**. It is *not* documented as one identical test sequence across the listed launchers. In particular, a 20 K LH₂ service specification, a 77 K alloy paper, and a room-temperature weld result cannot be combined into a claimed program-specific 20 K qualification without a report that actually connects them. (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000078, pqac-00000079, pqac-00000065, pqac-00000038)

The treatment reportedly retained conventional-aging yield strength while substantially improving ductility and eFT, allowing previously rejected material to meet simulated service requirements. contexts.context: The excerpt establishes the SLWT context and gives one explicit fracture-toughness acceptance value: alloy 2195 had to achieve cryogenic fracture toughness (CFT) greater than 30 ksi√in. It states that cryogenic fracture tests were performed for lot acceptance, while tensile and stress-corrosion-cracking tests were performed at ambient temperature, but it does not specify the exact cryogenic or ambient test temperatures. The excerpt defines FTR as “fracture toughness ratio,” yet provides no numerical cryogenic-to-ambient ratio requirement or measured ratio values. It reports that suitable processing and heat treatment can produce higher fracture toughness at cryogenic than at ambient temperature. Both multistep heating-rate-controlled (MSRC) aging and the two-step treatment identified as No. 24 substantially improved CFT; the comparative data indicate that these treatments enabled compliance with the 30 ksi√in minimum. Treatment No. 24 was 132 °C/20 hr followed by 138 °C/40 hr, and it produced very limited T1 precipitate growth. contexts.context: The excerpt is the NASA/TM-2002-211546 report abstract on artificial aging of alloy 2195 for the Super Lightweight Tank. It states that Marshall Space Flight Center’s original multistep heating-rate-controlled (MSRC) aging method enhanced cryogenic fracture toughness (eFT) and reduced the scatter in toughness values by controlling the location and size of strengthening T1 precipitates. Because production furnaces could not reliably maintain the original 0.6 °C (1 °F)/hr heating rate, the process was redesigned as a two-step treatment: 132 °C (270 °F) for 20 hours followed by 138 °C (280 °F) for 40 hours. The proposed microstructural explanation is that aging promotes T1 nucleation and growth in the matrix while suppressing it at subgrain boundaries. It attributes NASA’s use partly to AA2219’s practicality and availability and notes favorable solution-treated-and-aged properties at 500–600 °F, as well as suitability for welded fuel tanks across a broad stated temperature range. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies Boddorff’s document as NASA/TM–20250007133, “Choosing the Right Stuff: Material Selection for Liquid Hydrogen Aircraft Cryotanks,” published in July 2025. It provides a high-level comparison of metallic and composite cryotank construction for commercial liquid-hydrogen aircraft. Metallic materials are characterized as having high damage tolerance, mature large-scale manufacturing, good durability, and low cost; composites offer high specific properties and may better accommodate complex, conformal internal tank shapes. The report highlights the need for cryotanks to withstand approximately 10^4 thermomechanical cycles, with low hydrogen permeation and embrittlement susceptibility, long fatigue life, and low crack-growth rates. It identifies high-strength aluminum alloys and carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer composites as the principal candidate materials, while composite/metallic liner concepts and fiber-metal laminates are excluded or considered immature because of unresolved coefficient-of-thermal-expansion mismatch or insufficient research maturity. The excerpt does not provide the requested NASA Mital, Gyekenyesi, Arnold, Sullivan, or Witzell references; specific 2219/2195 alloy test results; 77 K versus 20 K measurements; fracture or leak-before-break indices; or European Airbus/DLR trial data. contexts.context: NASA/TM—2006-214346 notes that the Shuttle External Tank stored ~228,000 lb LH₂ at ~2 atm for ~8.5 minutes. Its pressurized structure changed from 2219 aluminum to Al-Li 2195, yielding higher strength and slightly lower density (Bickley and Schwinghamer, 1999). contexts.question: How have launch-vehicle, spacecraft and aircraft programs documented the use of cryogenic mechanical testing to select and qualify aluminum alloys for cryogenic propellant tanks? contexts.context: NASA CR-145140 (1977), Witzell, *Evaluation of Mechanical Property Data on 2219 Aluminum Alloy and Application…*, documents 2219-T87 and weld testing for LH₂ tanks. A cryostat-equipped tensile, fracture, and fatigue system tested specimens at −320°F (~77 K) and −423°F (~20 K), including LT/TL orientations and welds. The report covers an 88-page, NASA Langley contract study (NAS1-14048; NASA CR-145140; CASD-NAS-77-008).

contexts.context: The excerpt documents cryogenic structural testing mainly for composite LH₂ aircraft/launch tanks, not aluminum-alloy selection. X–33’s two 8.7 × 6.1 × 4.3 m linerless graphite/epoxy tanks underwent NASA Marshall pressure and mechanical-load testing with LH₂ in November 1999; failure after drain/purge resulted from microcracking, hydrogen infiltration, liquefied nitrogen, and reduced bondline strength/toughness. Findings were reported in the NASA Marshall report (2000) and Grimsley et al. (2001). NGLT quarter-scale tanks (4.6 m × 1.8 m) were pressurized to 779 kPa and planned for ~40 chill/refill/load cycles (Glass 2004; Sharke 2004; McKinney and Neiwert 2004). No 77/20 K values or fracture-toughness ratios are given.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents Shuttle ET/SLWT alloy and weld qualification, but gives no cryogenic test temperatures or fracture-toughness measurements. Wide-panel tensile specimens used full-size repairs in 20-inch-wide, 52-inch-long panels to assess load redistribution and residual stress; planishing produced “114% Recovery” at 20 ksi for 2195/4043, repair level R5. Al 2195 repairs had lower mechanical properties, prompting process changes. FSW produced joints at about 80% of base-metal strength versus 40–50% for fusion welding. SLWT initially used Al 2195, then reverted selected domes/ogive components to Al 2219. FSW was introduced on ET-132 and completed all barrels by ET-134.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns Mitsubishi Heavy Industries’ 2005 development of friction stir welding (FSW) for H-IIA/H-IIB-type rocket propellant tanks. It identifies the material only generically as a lightweight aluminum-lithium alloy and does not provide an alloy designation, temper, composition, or a clear distinction between H-IIA, H-IIB, and later H3 tank alloys. The bobbin-tool FSW process was developed to provide an internal self-reacting force, eliminating the need for large internal backing pads and enabling both axial and circumferential welding. MHI’s 2000 work established tool geometry, part holding, and basic weld conditions. A roughly 1 m-diameter subscale tank received a circumferential weld in 2001, and its weld strength was checked by pressurization to a stress exceeding 1.5 times the expected flight-service stress. Prototype equipment then demonstrated axial welding in 2002 and circumferential welding in 2004 on a 4 m-diameter component matching the standard H-IIA rocket tank diameter. The passage mentions joint characteristics and nondestructive inspection, but it does not report actual cryogenic mechanical testing, test temperatures, comparison with service temperatures, or detailed weld qualification criteria. Thus, it supports general FSW qualification and overpressure testing, not exact alloy identification or cryogenic validation.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Witzell’s verification and data-generation approach for thin-wall 2219 aluminum liquid-hydrogen tankage. Chemically milled base-metal fracture specimens were nominally 0.040 in thick, while welded specimens were 0.125 in thick and retained their as-received thickness. Static fracture and cyclic flaw-growth information was sought for both base material and weldments at room temperature and 20 K (-423°F), but the excerpt does not provide numerical tensile strength, fracture-toughness, S-N fatigue, fatigue-crack-growth, or lifetime results. Verification testing compared three inspection/proof-test concepts: no proof test during tank life, one proof test before first flight, and proof testing every 1000 flights. Because no established thin-wall flaw-screening method was available, proof stress was selected somewhat arbitrarily as 1.03 times room-temperature operating stress. The simplified cyclic stress range was 145–310 MPa for base metal and 57.9–124 MPa for weldments. The report notes insufficient evidence concerning sustained crack growth in liquid hydrogen and recommends generating additional data before committing to long-term liquid-hydrogen storage designs. Leak-before-break conclusions and exact NASA/CR-145140 lifetime recommendations are not contained in this excerpt.

contexts.context: This excerpt addresses static fracture behavior and leak-before-failure observations for 2219-T87 aluminum weldments, rather than the full NASA liquid-hydrogen aircraft study requested. It reports tests at approximately 78 K and 20 K, with specimens 1.60, 2.67, and 7.62 mm thick. At 78 K, all thin-gage specimens (1.60 and 2.67 mm) leaked before failure; the 7.62 mm specimens could fracture before leakage only at stresses at or above yield. At 20 K, leakage remained the predominant failure mode, although fracture was observed at slightly below yield in some cases. One 7.62 mm specimen fractured below 0.90 engineering yield strength; its calculated Irwin K was 25.2 MN/m^(3/2), increased by roughly 10% after back-surface magnification, but the authors rejected this toughness value because the fracture stress exceeded the weld-nugget yield strength. The room-temperature results similarly indicate that elastic fracture was virtually nonexistent through 7.62 mm thickness. contexts.context: The excerpt summarizes the additional mechanical-property testing performed for thin-gage 2219 aluminum intended for liquid-hydrogen tankage. Because existing information was inadequate, the study generated strength, fracture toughness, cyclic crack-growth, and fatigue data, especially at 20 K. Tensile properties increased at cryogenic temperature, while weldments had substantially lower strength than the base metal; base-metal elongation showed no degradation at 20 K, whereas weld elongation was somewhat lower. Static plane-stress fracture toughness also increased from room temperature to 20 K. Reported room-temperature versus 20 K toughness values were approximately 50 versus 69 for longitudinal base metal, 47 versus 68 transverse, 33 versus 45 for welds, and 33 versus 47 for chem-milled welds, in the stated Kc units. Welds were less tough than the base material, and chem milling had little effect on weld toughness. Fatigue results indicated longer life at 20 K for corresponding stresses than room-temperature results for thicker material, but welded material performed worse than base metal. Cyclic crack-growth data were difficult and expensive to obtain in liquid hydrogen because crack measurement required visual observation. In welded specimens tested over a 57.9–124.1 MPa spectrum, no breakthroughs occurred before 100,000 flights. The excerpt does not provide 77 K data, explicit S-N tables, detailed lifetime recommendations, proof criteria, or a complete leak-before-break analysis.

Chem-milled 2219-T87 parent material was reduced from 0.318 cm to approximately 0.127 cm, while weldments were produced using conventional gas-tungsten-arc techniques on 0.318-cm material; additional thin welded specimens came from a Convair study. Center-notched specimens were tested in longitudinal and transverse grain directions for the parent material and in GTA-welded material. Tests used tension-tension precracking, room-temperature and liquid-hydrogen conditions, ascending loads, and a servo-controlled hydraulic system; liquid-hydrogen testing used a cryostat with a viewing port. The excerpt explicitly mentions room temperature and 4 K testing, but does not provide exact 77 K and 20 K results. Analytical work calculated Paris-law coefficients (C and n) and estimated cyclic threshold intensity values, with ΔK₀ reported to increase as temperature decreased for parent material. Verification tests found crack-through at approximately 2,400–3,675 cycles for most liquid-hydrogen specimens, whereas welded specimens under the cited lower stress spectrum did not break through in fewer than 100,000 cycles. No tensile-property tables, S-N curves, complete fracture-toughness values, lifetime recommendations, or explicit leak-before-break proof criteria appear in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt gives the leak-before-break material index as KIc²/σf (rendered in the source as “KIc 2/σf”), where KIc is fracture toughness and σf is material strength. Its purpose is to ensure that, at the maximum pressure carried by the tank, a crack grows stably until it penetrates both the inner and outer tank surfaces, producing a detectable leak before catastrophic rupture. The related yield-before-break index is KIc/σf; it requires the stress needed to propagate a critical flaw to exceed the stress needed to yield the material, allowing stable, detectable deformation. The excerpt also notes that both indices must be balanced against pressure capability and tank mass, since excessively low strength can require an impractically thick and heavy wall. It identifies continuous-fiber-reinforced polymer composites as offering very high specific strength, while discontinuously reinforced aluminum composites may provide a lower-cost, comparatively low-permeability alternative. contexts.context: The excerpt provides general friction stir welding (FSW) information but does not identify Falcon 9 alloys as Al-Li 2198 or 2195, nor does it discuss Atlas V Centaur, Delta IV welds, Vulcan qualification, cryogenic metal coupon data, LOX/RP-1, or LH2. It states that an FSW joint contains four microstructural regions: the nugget or stirred zone, thermo-mechanically affected zone, heat-affected zone, and parent/base material. The stirred zone undergoes severe tool-pin stirring, plastic deformation, dynamic recrystallization, and formation of fine equiaxed grains. FSW temperatures may reach approximately 0.75–0.8 of the base material’s melting temperature. In aluminum matrix composites, stirring can redistribute clustered reinforcement particles, round sharp particle edges, reduce particle size, and modify particle spacing, distribution, morphology, and size. The excerpt also notes that appropriate process parameters and heat input promote material flow, uniform particle distribution, and improved joint quality. These are generic process and microstructure observations and cannot substantiate claims about specific launch-vehicle alloys, weld practices, cryogenic qualification, or public material-test data.

contexts.context: For the Shuttle Super Lightweight Tank (SLWT), thermally stabilized (TS) aging treatment No. 8 was selected after tensile and fracture-toughness evaluation. Lot-acceptance testing measured strength and fracture toughness at ambient and cryogenic temperatures in relevant orientations; acceptance required “FTR greater than one,” where FTR = cryogenic fracture toughness/ambient fracture toughness. Rejected plates showed low CFT or FTR. Excessive grain-boundary T1 precipitates reduced toughness. A multistep aging treatment improved CFT at equivalent yield strength, supporting avoidance of costly cryogenic proof testing.

contexts.context: Lockheed Martin/NASA’s Al-Li 2195 FSW tank-development study tested over 300 ft of 0.320-in plate, including 2195-to-2195 and 2219-to-2195 joints. Tensile tests used room temperature and −423°F (about 20 K, liquid-hydrogen temperature); SCT fracture-toughness, NDE, metallography, photostress, and repair-panel tests supplemented them. Over 300 mechanical, 30 SCT/SS, and four repair tests were completed. FSW showed higher strength, elongation, cryogenic enhancement, and toughness than fusion welds; weld strength approached parent material at −423°F, with a cryogenic/RT strength ratio of 1.6. No volumetric defects were found.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses static fracture and leak-before-fail behavior of 2219-T87 aluminum weldments, rather than reproducing the NASA CR-145140/Witzell 1977 tensile-strength or plane-stress Kc table requested. It reports applied-stress versus flaw-size results at room temperature, 78 K, and 20 K for 1.60, 2.67, and 7.62 mm weldments. Thin specimens generally leaked or broke through before fracture; in the 7.62 mm material, fracture before leakage occurred only at stresses near or above yield at room temperature and 78 K. At 20 K, fracture could occur slightly below engineering yield, but the cited 7.62 mm specimen had an Irwin K of 25.2 MN/m^3/2, equivalent to 25.2 MPa√m, and the authors explicitly considered that toughness value invalid because the stress exceeded weld-nugget yield strength. Thus, these are conditional calculated Irwin K values for weldments, not necessarily valid plane-stress Kc or KIC values. The excerpt does not provide the requested exact Kc values of 50 and 69 MPa√m, the parent tensile pairs 385/460 and 506/684 MPa, the TIG-weld pairs 135/262 and 249/458 MPa, or confirmation that 77 K data were only imported surface-crack plots. Those details would need verification in the cited NASA report and its tables/figures.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: How have launch-vehicle, spacecraft and aircraft programs documented the use of cryogenic mechanical testing to select and qualify aluminum alloys for cryogenic propellant tanks? Examples: the Space Shuttle external tank and super-lightweight tank (2219 to 2195 Al-Li), the SLS core stage (2219), Delta IV, Atlas V and Vulcan, Falcon 9 (Al-Li with friction stir welding), Ariane 5 and 6, H-IIA and H3, Chinese launch vehicles (2219, 5A06, Al-Li), and liquid-hydrogen aircraft tank studies (NASA, Airbus, DLR). For each, give the test temperatures used (77 K vs 20 K), the properties measured (for example the cryogenic-to-room-temperature fracture toughness ratio, weld strength, leak-before-break), and NASA technical reports or conference papers with citations, DOIs or NTRS numbers.

# Cryogenic aluminum-alloy evidence for propellant tanks

**The distinction is between a material test and a tank’s operating temperature.** Liquid nitrogen testing near **77 K** (−196 °C, −320 °F) is common in alloy screening; liquid-hydrogen testing near **20 K** (−253 °C, −423 °F) addresses the colder service condition. A paper specifying a 20 K hydrogen tank does **not**, by itself, establish that its alloy coupons were tested at 20 K. The public record is detailed for some NASA programs but does not support a uniform, vehicle-by-vehicle list of 77 K and 20 K qualification results. (chen2002cryogenicfracturetoughness pages 12-16, witzell1977evaluationofmechanical pages 1-4, merino2017ariane6tanksand pages 1-2)

| Program or study | What the documentation establishes | Specimen-test temperature and measured property; source |
|---|---|---|
| **Space Shuttle external tank and super-lightweight tank (SLWT)** | The original tank used **2219**; **2195 Al–Li** replaced it in substantial portions of the lighter tank. Production acceptance encompassed material allowables, welds, inspection and proof tests, not merely parent-metal strength. Welding difficulties later led some domes and ogives back to 2219. | Chen and colleagues tested 2195 fracture specimens at **ambient and 77 K**, measuring strength and cryogenic fracture toughness; the reported SLWT minimum cryogenic toughness was **30 ksi√in**. Separately, a published lot-acceptance guideline was **fracture-toughness ratio, FTR = cryogenic/ambient toughness >1**. For lot 950M029B, conventional aging gave **25.40/30.04 = 0.85**; two-step aging gave **33.74/30.44 = 1.11**, in ksi√in at 77 K/ambient. The treatment improved the cryogenic value while controlling detrimental subgrain-boundary T₁ precipitates. These are **77 K results, not 20 K toughness results**. NASA/TM-2002-211546; NASA/TM-2002-211547; Chen *et al.*, DOI **10.1361/105994998770347576**; Chen and Stanton, DOI **10.1557/proc-551-285**. (worden2011externaltankprogramlegacy pages 1-3, worden2011externaltankprogramlegacy pages 5-9, worden2011externaltankprogramlegacy pages 13-17, chen1998theeffectsof pages 1-2, chen2002cryogenicfracturetoughness pages 12-16, chen1998artificialeffectson pages 18-25, chen2002cryogenicfracturetoughness media ed30da98, chen2002cryogenicfracturetoughness pages 20-23) |
| **Shuttle-related 2195 friction-stir-weld development** | Weld qualification is distinct from the foregoing plate-lot toughness criterion. Lockheed Martin tested 2195/2195 and 2219/2195 combinations, including surface-crack-tension specimens. | **Room temperature and −423 °F (≈20 K)** tensile tests were reported. The paper describes a **1.6 cryogenic/room-temperature weld-strength enhancement factor**, weld strength approaching parent-metal strength at 20 K, and improved surface-crack-tension performance relative to fusion welding; **1.6 is a strength ratio, not FTR**. Kinchen, Li and Adams, “Mechanical Properties of Friction Stir Welds in Al2195-T8” (1999). The ET program history reports approximately **80% base-metal-strength** FSW joints versus **40–50%** for fusion welds, without assigning those summary percentages to a particular test temperature. (kinchen1999mechanicalpropertiesof pages 1-3, worden2011externaltankprogramlegacy pages 13-17) |
| **SLS core stage** | SLS uses **2219** for its cryogenic tank structure; development work also investigated possible 2195 dome gores. A NASA safety assessment examined the short-transverse weakness of commercial *thick 2219-T87 plate*, an important caveat to using favorable longitudinal properties as design allowables. | Hales reports **full-thickness short-transverse tensile tests at 20 °C, −196 °C (≈77 K), and −253 °C (≈20 K)**, measuring yield strength, ultimate strength and fracture elongation. Through-thickness variations and intermetallic-particle clustering affected fracture. This is **plate characterization**, not a published 20 K toughness ratio for a completed SLS tank or its FSW seams. **NASA/TM-20230006220**, NESC-RP-21-01721; related Medders *et al.*, **NASA/TM-20230018439**. (hales2023metallurgicalfactorsthat pages 1-6, hales2023metallurgicalfactorsthat media 31c7836c, hales2023metallurgicalfactorsthat pages 9-11, medders2023shorttransversetensilefracture pages 1-5, qiu2021researchprogressof pages 6-8) |
| **Delta IV; Atlas V/Centaur; Vulcan** | Reviews discuss FSW in launch-tank manufacture and identify **Al–Li** use in Atlas V’s Centaur. Those statements do not identify a common alloy, test method or qualification campaign for all three vehicles. | **No attributable 77 K/20 K coupon-property table, FTR, or leak-before-break demonstration for these named programs was established in the retrieved papers.** Their use of cryogenic propellants cannot supply a missing specimen-test temperature. (ablakatov2022aluminumlithiumalloystypes pages 4-5, ablakatov2022aluminumlithiumalloystypes pages 2-4, henson2018materialsforlaunch pages 39-42) |
| **Falcon 9** | A published review identifies **Al–Li 2198** sheet/plate in its stages; another describes friction-stir-welded aluminum-alloy tank manufacture. Falcon 9’s stage propellants are **LOX/kerosene rather than liquid hydrogen**: Shuttle LH₂-tank 20 K results must not be assigned to it. | **No Falcon-9-specific 77 K or 20 K tensile, fracture-toughness, weld-strength or leak-before-break dataset was verified** in the retrieved literature. Review: Ablakatov *et al.*, DOI **10.31643/2022/6445.34**. (ablakatov2022aluminumlithiumalloystypes pages 4-5, henson2018materialsforlaunch pages 39-42) |
| **Ariane 5** | A 1996 weldment paper states that **AA2219 was selected for Ariane V**; it studies 2219 weld microstructure, hardness, tensile properties and weld efficiency. | That paper **does not document a 77 K or 20 K Ariane-5 tank-coupon qualification series**. Rao *et al.*, DOI **10.1007/BF02744827**. (rao1996structurepropertycorrelationon pages 1-5) |
| **Ariane 6** | An MT Aerospace conference paper specifies, for the upper-module tanks, **2195 cylinder/dome segments** and **2219 rings and manhole hardware**; its lower-module components instead specify **2195 domes** and **2219 cylinders and rings**. It describes FSW and development/qualification activities, including panel and structural testing. | **20 K to room temperature for LH₂** and **90 K to room temperature for LOX** are stated **tank design ranges**, *not disclosed coupon-test temperatures*. The paper does not furnish a 77 K/20 K alloy toughness ratio or test matrix. Merino *et al.*, “Ariane 6—Tanks & Structures for the New European Launcher,” **Deutscher Luft- und Raumfahrtkongress 2017, Document ID 450255**. (merino2017ariane6tanksand pages 1-2, merino2017ariane6tanksand pages 2-4, merino2017ariane6tanksand pages 6-7) |
| **H-IIA, H-IIB and H3** | A Mitsubishi Heavy Industries paper describes H-IIB tank/FSW development based on H-IIA hardware. A subscale welded tank was pressure-tested to **more than 1.5 times expected flight stress**; it also reports larger-scale axial and circumferential weld demonstrations. | Its **−253 °C LH₂** and **−183 °C LOX** values identify **propellant service environments**, not recorded tensile or toughness coupon-test temperatures. The accessible paper does not substantiate a particular H-IIA/H3 aluminum grade or a 77 K/20 K FTR. Goto *et al.*, “Highly Reliable Tank Structure of H-IIB Launch Vehicle” (2005). **H3-specific qualification values were not verified.** (goto2005highlyreliabletank pages 2-4, goto2005highlyreliabletank pages 1-2) |
| **Chinese launch vehicles** | A review traces tank alloys **5A06 → 2A14/2219** and explicitly identifies **2219** for the **CZ-5 LH₂ tank**; it discusses weld defects and residual stress as qualification concerns. | It recommends more systematic properties testing at and below **77 K**, but supplies **no attributable CZ-5 77 K-versus-20 K coupon series**, toughness ratio, or leak-before-break result. Nor does it establish that a particular Chinese launcher adopted **Al–Li** in place of these grades. Qiu *et al.*, DOI **10.3390/met11071101**. (qiu2021researchprogressof pages 6-8) |
| **NASA thin-wall LH₂ *aircraft* tank investigation** | Unlike a conceptual tank comparison, Convair’s NASA-sponsored study generated **2219-T87 parent-metal and TIG-weld** data for a hypothetical aircraft tank and used flaw-growth calculations to examine service life. | **Room-temperature and actual 20 K LH₂-cryostat tests** measured yield/ultimate tensile strength, *plane-stress* crack resistance **Kc**, fatigue and crack growth. Parent-metal yield/ultimate rose from approximately **385/460 to 506/684 MPa**; weld values rose from **135/262 to 249/458 MPa**. Longitudinal parent-metal **Kc: 50→69 MPa√m**; weld **Kc: 33→45 MPa√m**. These must **not** be relabeled plane-strain *K*IC. The report also reproduces −320 °F and −423 °F surface-/through-crack information; its newly reported tensile and Kc comparisons are specifically room temperature versus **20 K**. Witzell, **NASA/CR-145140** (1977). (witzell1977evaluationofmechanical pages 1-4, witzell1977evaluationofmechanical pages 15-17, witzell1977evaluationofmechanical pages 17-20, witzell1977evaluationofmechanical pages 24-28, witzell1977evaluationofmechanical pages 39-42) |
| **NASA aircraft material screening; Airbus and DLR studies** | NASA’s **2050-T84** comparison tests show why a 77 K material screen is not an LH₂-temperature qualification: compact-tension results vary by crack orientation, and the authors specifically request future **20 K** testing. Aircraft tank design papers and Airbus Cryoplane concepts address structural sizing, thermal insulation and operation, rather than establishing Airbus/DLR alloy-coupon qualification data. | At **75 °F versus −320 °F (≈77 K)**, 2050 conditional toughness **KQJIC** was **38.4→32.4 ksi√in (L–T)**, **24.8→28.2 (T–L)** and **37.7→44.4 (L–S)**: ratios **0.84, 1.14 and 1.18**. **All failed the cited ASTM toughness-validity requirements**; they are comparative, not certified *K*IC values. **NASA/TM-2011-217163**. Gomez and Smith’s aircraft sizing study, DOI **10.1016/j.ast.2019.105438**, specifies a **22.5 K modeled tank condition**, not a specimen test. The retrieved Airbus/DLR-related accounts do **not** provide a verified proprietary 77 K/20 K aluminum-alloy test matrix. (hafley2011evaluationofaluminum pages 24-28, hafley2011evaluationofaluminum pages 1-7, hafley2011evaluationofaluminum pages 28-34, gomez2019liquidhydrogenfuel pages 3-4, tzoumakis2024multiphysicsdigitalmodel pages 2-4) |

**Leak-before-break requires separate evidence.** NASA’s aircraft-tank review, **NASA/TM-2006-214346**, presents the material-selection indices *K*IC/σf for yield-before-break and **(*K*IC)²/σf** for leak-before-break. An index is **not** evidence that a particular launcher passed a pressurized, flawed-tank test. Earlier 2219 pressure-vessel work instead explicitly studied proof loads, ligament penetration and residual cyclic life across conditions down to **20 K** (**NASA/CR-135036**); weldment flaw tests at about **78 K and 20 K** observed leakage before fracture in many configurations but also identified thickness- and stress-dependent exceptions. These studies support examining flaws, welds, wall thickness and operating load together rather than declaring an alloy intrinsically “leak-before-break.” (mital2006reviewofcurrent pages 24-27, finger1976prooftestcriteria pages 1-6, masters1974deepflawsin pages 44-48)

**Bottom line:** The most traceable progression is **77 K plate screening and SLWT 2195 lot acceptance → 20 K testing of selected welds, thick 2219 plate and aircraft-tank materials → component proof, flaw-growth and leak assessment**. It is *not* documented as one identical test sequence across the listed launchers. In particular, a 20 K LH₂ service specification, a 77 K alloy paper, and a room-temperature weld result cannot be combined into a claimed program-specific 20 K qualification without a report that actually connects them. (chen1998theeffectsof pages 1-2, kinchen1999mechanicalpropertiesof pages 1-3, hales2023metallurgicalfactorsthat media 31c7836c, merino2017ariane6tanksand pages 1-2, witzell1977evaluationofmechanical pages 1-4)

info.query: How have launch-vehicle, spacecraft and aircraft programs documented the use of cryogenic mechanical testing to select and qualify aluminum alloys for cryogenic propellant tanks? Examples: the Space Shuttle external tank and super-lightweight tank (2219 to 2195 Al-Li), the SLS core stage (2219), Delta IV, Atlas V and Vulcan, Falcon 9 (Al-Li with friction stir welding), Ariane 5 and 6, H-IIA and H3, Chinese launch vehicles (2219, 5A06, Al-Li), and liquid-hydrogen aircraft tank studies (NASA, Airbus, DLR). For each, give the test temperatures used (77 K vs 20 K), the properties measured (for example the cryogenic-to-room-temperature fracture toughness ratio, weld strength, leak-before-break), and NASA technical reports or conference papers with citations, DOIs or NTRS numbers.
